label: Claude Fable 5.2
output:
# My van almost caught fire. Please go look at yours.

This isn't a fun one, sorry. No before-and-afters today.

On Wednesday, October 28, the cable that runs between my batteries and my inverter melted while I was drying a dog. Nobody was hurt. The dog is fine, I'm fine, and the van didn't burn down. But I'm off the road for at least three weeks, and what the electrician showed me afterwards scared me enough that I want every one of you who works out of a van to read this and then go open up wherever your batteries live.

I'll say this now and again at the bottom: I'm a dog groomer, not an electrician. Everything electrical in this post is what an electrician showed me, plus what I've read since, written down the way I understand it. If something here makes you nervous about your own van, good. Get someone qualified to look at it.

## What happened

It was about 2:15 in the afternoon. I was parked in a client's driveway in Bedford, drying Moose. Moose is a Bernese, which means the dryer was on high and was going to be for a while.

I smelled hot plastic first. I thought it was the dryer motor, because dryer motors die and that's what it smells like when they do. So I kept going for a bit, which I'm not proud of. Then I saw smoke coming out of the bench seat, and the bench seat is where my batteries are.

I killed the battery switch and got Moose out the side door, still damp. He was thrilled, honestly. Then I went back for the extinguisher and used a bit of it. I'm still not sure I needed to. When I got the seat open, the lug on the end of the positive cable was black and the cable's jacket had melted back about 3 cm.

After that I sat on the client's front steps and shook. Moose's mom brought me a coffee and sat with me until I stopped. If you're reading this, thank you. I don't think I said it properly at the time.

## My setup, so you can compare

- 3000 watt inverter
- Two 200Ah lithium batteries
- 12 volt system
- Built in spring 2025 by Coastline Van Fitouts

A lot of you have something very close to this. It's a pretty standard grooming van build.

## What the electrician found

Priya from Sackville Marine Electric came out and went through the whole thing with me. She found three things wrong with the wiring, plus one thing that isn't wiring at all.

### 1. The cable was way too thin

The cable from my batteries to my inverter was 4 AWG. Priya says that for a 3000 watt inverter on a 12 volt system, it should have been 2/0 (people say "two aught"). I looked it up afterwards and 2/0 has roughly three times as much copper in it as 4 AWG. It's a completely different cable, not just the next size up.

It took me a while to understand why that matters so much.

Amps are what heat up a wire, and you get amps by dividing watts by volts. My dryer pulls somewhere around 1800 to 2000 watts. Plugged into the wall at home, that's 2000 divided by 120 volts, so about 17 amps. Normal extension cord territory.

In the van, that power is coming out of 12 volt batteries. So on the battery side of the inverter it's 2000 divided by 12, which is about 167 amps. Same dryer, ten times the amps. And sometimes my water heater is running too. The inverter is rated for 3000 watts, which works out to 250 amps flat out.

So on a normal working day, somewhere between 150 and 250 amps was going through a cable that was never meant to carry that. It did it for a year and a half, and then one day it didn't.

### 2. The lug was crimped with pliers, or maybe a hammer

The lug is the metal ring on the end of the cable that bolts onto the battery or the inverter. It's supposed to be squeezed onto the cable with a proper crimping tool so the copper and the lug are basically one solid piece.

Mine, on the positive end, looked like it had been squashed on with pliers or hit with a hammer. Priya couldn't say which, just that it wasn't done with a crimper. A bad crimp means a bad connection, and a bad connection is where the heat builds up. That's exactly where mine burned.

I never saw it because there was a neat piece of heat-shrink over the top hiding it.

### 3. The fuse was the wrong distance from the battery, and couldn't have saved me anyway

I did have a main fuse. It was a 300 amp ANL fuse, mounted about 90 cm along the cable from the battery. Priya said it should be within roughly 18 cm.

The way I understand it, the fuse only protects what comes after it. Every bit of cable between the battery and the fuse has nothing protecting it. If that stretch rubs through somewhere and touches metal, nothing stops the battery from dumping everything it has into it. I had 90 cm of that.

And a 300 amp fuse doesn't do anything until there's more than 300 amps going through it. My cable was cooking at 150 to 250, so the fuse was never going to blow. That one really got me, because I assumed that if there was a fuse, I was covered.

Priya's repair swaps the ANL for a Class T fuse. From what I gather, that's the type you want with lithium batteries because of how much current they can throw out if something shorts.

### 4. No smoke detector in the back

There's one in the cab, which came with the van. There was nothing in the back, where the batteries, the inverter, the dryer, the dog and I all are. I found out by smell and then by seeing smoke. If I'd had my back turned or headphones in, I don't know how long it would have taken me to notice.

## The photos

Priya pulled up my damage photos on her phone next to thermal camera shots of her own van, taken while it was running the same kind of load mine runs every day. Hers barely gets warm, with the same sort of power going through it. The difference is wild. Seeing them side by side is what made it sink in that this wasn't bad luck or a freak thing. The cable was undersized and the crimp was bad, and it had been heating up every time I dried a dog.

## Tidy is not the same as right

I trusted this build because it looked tidy. The cables were routed neatly, everything was zip-tied and labelled, and there was heat-shrink on every end. I opened that bench seat plenty of times and thought it looked professional.

But tidy is not the same as right. I had no idea what size the cable should be, so I had no way of knowing it was wrong. I didn't know what a good crimp looked like, and I couldn't have seen mine anyway. I didn't know fuse distance was even a thing.

## About the builder

I'm not writing this to trash anybody. The facts are that Coastline Van Fitouts did the build in spring 2025, and the things above are what a marine electrician found when she opened it up. I've texted Darren three times and sent one email. I haven't heard back yet. If I do, I'll say so here.

You can make up your own minds.

## If you're about to pay someone to build your van

Tasha, this part is for you, and for anyone else getting quotes right now.

Before you pay a deposit, ask for these in writing. It doesn't matter who the builder is.

1. **What size cable goes between the batteries and the inverter, and how long is the run?** An actual size, like "2/0", not "heavy duty".
2. **What type of main fuse, what rating, and how far from the battery will it be mounted?**
3. **What tool do you use to crimp the lugs?** Ask if they'll send photos of the crimps before the heat-shrink goes on.
4. **Will I get a wiring diagram when I pick it up?**
5. **Is there a smoke detector in the working area?**

A good builder will just answer these, and plenty will be happy you asked. If someone gets weird about putting cable sizes in writing, that tells you something.

Then, if you can, pay an electrician for half an hour to read the answers. It'll cost a lot less than what I'm paying now.

## A check you can do on your own van

You can do all of this without tools and without knowing anything. You're only looking and writing things down.

**First:** turn off your battery switch and unplug from shore power. Take off rings and bracelets. Don't put a wrench or anything metal on the battery terminals. The switch only turns off what comes after it, and the batteries themselves are always live.

1. **Find the cable from your battery to your inverter and read it.** The size is printed along the jacket. Write it down.
2. **Find your inverter's manual, or google the model number.** They nearly all have a table saying what cable and fuse size to use. See if yours matches.
3. **Find your main fuse.** Write down what type it is and the number stamped on it. Then measure along the cable from the battery's positive terminal to the fuse. Priya's number was about 18 cm. Mine was 90.
4. **Look at every lug you can see.** Check the battery end, the fuse, the switch and the inverter end. Is the heat-shrink browned, shiny, wrinkled or pulled back? Is the metal discoloured? Is any plastic nearby melted or warped?
5. **Give each cable a gentle wiggle where it goes into its lug.** It shouldn't move in there at all.
6. **Smell it.** I mean it. Hot plastic has a smell, and it hangs around.
7. **Follow the cable.** Is it rubbing on a metal edge anywhere? Is it flopping around loose?
8. **Look up.** Is there a smoke detector back there? Does it work?
9. **Check your extinguisher.** Is the gauge in the green, and can you reach it from where you stand to groom?
10. **Find your battery switch with your eyes closed.** Mine is the reason this post isn't much worse. If yours is buried behind towels and shampoo, move the towels and shampoo.

If any of it looks off, or the numbers don't match the manual, take photos and send them to an electrician. Don't try to fix it yourself, and don't keep working out of the van and hope.

## Buy a $40 thermometer

I bought an infrared thermometer at Canadian Tire for 40 bucks. You point it at something and it tells you the temperature. I think everybody with an inverter should own one.

This is the one check you do with the power on. Run your dryer on high for ten minutes with the battery compartment open. Don't touch anything. Point the thermometer at each connection: the battery terminals, the fuse, the switch and where the cables go into the inverter. Then go along the cable itself. Apparently these things read wrong off shiny bare metal, so aim at the cable jacket or the heat-shrink right beside the lug.

I don't have a magic number for you, and I'm not going to invent one. What you're looking for is one spot that's much hotter than everything else, or anything hot enough that you wouldn't want to put your hand on it. A good electrician can tell you what's normal for your setup.

If I'd done this once in the last year and a half, I think I'd have caught it.

## One more time: I'm not an electrician

I groom dogs. I've written this as carefully as I can and checked the numbers, but it's secondhand. Please don't rewire anything because of a blog post. Use it to work out what to ask, then get a professional to look at your van. I'd go with a marine electrician if you can find one, because they deal with this kind of battery setup all the time.

## Where I'm at

The repair quote is $4,200. That covers rewiring the main cable runs, a new fuse block and the Class T fuse. It's three weeks minimum because the parts are on order.

I've cancelled 31 appointments so far. Insurance says "maybe", and the adjuster is coming Thursday.

I'm scared, honestly. That van is my whole income and rent is due on the 1st. I keep doing the math and it keeps coming out the same. I'm also aware of how much worse this could have gone, and I keep swinging between those two feelings about every twenty minutes.

I'll post again when the van's back and tell you what the insurance said and what the new wiring looks like. In the meantime, please go check your cable. Take a photo of the printing on it and send it to me if you want. I can't tell you if it's right, but I'd like to know you looked.

Give your dogs a squish from me.

---

**Notes before you post:**

- **Things I added:** these weren't in your notes, so run them past Priya if you get the chance:
  - 2/0 having about three times the copper of 4 AWG.
  - The comparison with the wall outlet at home, about 17 amps at 120 volts.
  - Why the 300A fuse never blew.
  - Why Class T suits lithium.
  - The tip about inverter manuals listing cable and fuse sizes.
  - Infrared thermometers reading wrong off shiny metal.
- **The date:** I used October 28 instead of "last week", since it's been two weeks now.
- **Names:** Coastline, Darren and Tasha are all named, as in your notes. They're easy to take out if you'd rather not.
